title: Are you guys using AI for the art part of the game too?
author: Icy_Masterpiece_4414
selftext:
I’m using it mainly for the code on unity. Maybe it’s my inability to set up the agent correctly, but I still think the art AI produces icks people off.  
I guess the human touch is still needed.  
But I do use it in some parts; textures are all hand painted, but things like cliffs and trees I asked AI to create a generator on blender. 

So far I paid more than 2k to have 10 3D models protagonists. I knew I wasn’t good enough to make them myself. They ended up nice. But the prices are truly a toll, especially for me: where I live the average wage is 1200€. I had to save for 3/4 months for those 10 models. And before the game comes out I need 10 more.  
And after the game is out I will periodically update it so I will need even more.

I don’t think I have the financial possibility to sustain this in long term. One of the reasons why I discovered AI development was precisely because I understood I couldn’t afford a dev. 

So I asked myself if I should turn on AI generated models, but I don’t know. Tried the free version of Tripo and the paid version of Meshy, and it seems like the technology has laid its basics, but it’s just no quite there.  
To not count the messy topology and I don’t know how to reto.

So far Claude seems great at some minor animations, even tho it needs some personal retouches as well. 

What about you guys? Do you use these softwares or you prefer your game to have that human touch?

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
Absolutely using AI for art, even though I used to do the whole thing before AI came along. But I also still manually edit every single piece to be up to my standards, adjust UV/mapping, do all the coloring by hand, and a slew of other custom model work that's part of my workflow (vertex painting, marking edges for two different custom shaders, baking AO, etc). But you can bet I'm not modeling everything from scratch. I basically just skip the first step of modeling (initial sculpt) and move right onto the retopo/cleanup/texture phases, which saves enough time on its own that it's great.

Would I use assets straight from AI production, however? No, not unless I was making a game for phones or an isometric camera that couldn't zoom in past like Diablo 2 or Octopath Traveler level. However mine is a over the shoulder open world and demands quality because people will see things close up and unintentional flaws will become immediately noticeable.

replies.author: croutonballs
replies.body: what is your general pipeline for doing this if you don’t mind me asking?

replies.author: CycleMother2006
replies.body:
The general pipeline is basically:

1. Quick sketch + prompt in an imagegen to produce reference image. Could try to do it with just a prompt but I have a particular style and my game is highly dependent on accurately detailed and shaped meshes for the lighting to run well, rather than detailed textures.
2. Put ref image into Tripo or Meshy. I'm sure other services could do well too, but I'm familiar with these and the requirements to get good models from them, as well as have specific workflows for fixing their particular issues. Meshy is the one that delivers more unique shapes with its models, but also has significantly more cleanup work in my experience (talking purely Smart Poly here).  Meshy is hands down the winner on just going for an accurate UHD model (I only use those for blender refs if I'm modeling a building or something and don't want to try and mentally think about proportions of what I'm modeling. So I'll gen a UHD model and then go into blender and start building a custom building kit out of primitives to match it. I just have had zero luck generating things like building kit pieces with accurate enough proportions to be usable in game so that is a generally manual process. If you were doing the same but using pbr textures, you could also bake down the UHD house's texturing to your manually built one (this is Retopo 101).
3. I have certain things I look for from the meshes. As you generate them you'll start to recognize instant signs of whether the mesh was good or not. Meshy does give 12 retries for each at higher plans so this can be pretty useful. Tripo just does its smart topo in batches of 4. It's kind of annoying. Tripo's topology is 100x better than Meshy's but it takes liberties and struggles to adhere to strong styles in comparison. Also likes to mirror things on sides it can't see, and Multiview is hit or miss.
4. Once I have an acceptable mesh, I throw it in blender and toggle on face orientation (to better view obvious defects). I fix the mesh. If there's a lot that's wrong with it, you probably shouldn't be using the mesh. But some more complex things might have a few dozen patches I have to fix. This could be missing faces, it could be tangled polys that need repositioning and/or cleanup as occasionally extra faces and vertices gen. It might just be that it decided to vanilla-ize the style and I have to adjust some proportions and tweak some parts. Because my style has very specific lighting and shader requirements, I'll usually have to simplify certain areas if it decided to add to fine of shifts (lighting can get weird in places where the faces wobble too much without a clear purpose.)
5. I then paint regions onto the mesh for UE to apply materials to the mesh at runtime depending on what I want something to be (for instance switching a tree's bark from a white birch to an ancient, worn oak or for shifting leaf colors during seasons.) I also do selective painting on edges where I want lines (see Guilty Gear / Sable dev talks if you're interested in that.) You can do outlining a lot of ways, but I like the consistency and lack of visual artifacts/ consistent readability that doing so on the mesh brings. It's the most tedious (far more so than just using a shader) but I'm a perfectionist and hate shimmering/flickering in games.
6. I bake AO after that, into the mesh. Nothing too special about that, though my settings are my own. Just look up 'baking AO into mesh' if you're interested. It's just another technique I've kind of adopted for a way to get more details onto my meshes that fit my style but don't require me to use heavy runtime gfx work or hd textures. You're basically calculating the AO in a certain environment out of game, and then always using that in game. Some studios just paint the AO directly onto their textures, but since I'm vertex painting instead that's not really an option for me.
7.  That's pretty much it. The steps get pretty fast when you're used to it, And depending on your requirements, half or more may be unnecessary, though you may have other required fixes like tending to whatever texture issues are present (this is one reason I vertex paint... because I didn't want to have to fix textures after cleaning up the mesh and suddenly having a bunch of mesh gaps and UV issues. Speaking of which, at some point you'll have to unwrap your UV if you're using textures. There are tools that can do this, or automated blender functions. The best is doing it yourself but.. that's a lesson in itself (though a short one).

comments.author: thatguywithimpact
comments.body:
Codex makes everything faster. But image gen is a whole other level. The other AI capabilities sometimes help a little sometimes a lot but image gen is completely other worldly superhuman ability that changes everything.

It generates such complex and intricate images in 5 seconds that you would never get to that quality with traditional rendering even with 10000x time and effort.

Redwood bark? Done, generated looks superior to any scanned texture.

The way I build things right now is I just ask for image gen to be target. Because it's just superior than any IRL image. And I built world from there. Shaders, textures, effects, height maps.

comments.author: stolenyourgf
comments.body: I work in 2D pixel art rather than 3D, so grain of salt, but the pattern that seems to work in both: use AI for the stuff players don't stare at, keep humans on the stuff they do. Protagonists are the face of your game, so I'd keep paying for those and use AI for props, rocks, clutter and variations. For AI meshes, the "not quite there" part is mostly topology and consistency. Blender's built-in QuadriFlow remesh (or Instant Meshes) plus re-texturing in your own hand-painted style gets them much closer to the rest of the game. Also worth asking your modeler if they'd do "cleanup + texture" on an AI base mesh for less than a full model.

replies.author: stolenyourgf
replies.body: Agree, locking the style down first matters most. Writing it as a one-page sheet helped me: canvas size, outline rule (black vs. dark hue-shifted), max colors per ramp, and one light direction. Every asset gets checked against that sheet before it goes in the game. Same as you with chat images: by the time it matches the sheet it's basically a reference. And learning traditional pixel art is what makes the editing pass fast, so it's time well spent.

If not -> AI.

comments.author: edwardkmett
comments.body:
Spend your effort on the part of the game where you have something to say and something you want to differentiate.   
  
For me back in the day that used to be game engine design. And even nowadays it is usually in the graphics pipeline, lighting system design, and clever pass structure involving crazy math and alternative rendering techniques. e.g. I like to use various forms of procedural content (in my case not necessarily AI generated, just procedural) because I lack a solid art asset management pipeline and don't have anything particular that I want to "say" on that front.

One way to think of it is you have a bounded amount of novelty and budget in both time and money for your game. How do you want to spend it?   
  
If AI let's you compress the amount of time you are spending on the uninteresting-to-you parts and let's you convey the part where you can connect to your users without distracting you or your users then that's the part that AI is for. Use it and get back to focusing on the part where you are able to engage with your audience in a novel way.

comments.author: AdHom
comments.body:
I use AI for art during development, while sticking to a strict design document that should allow fairly seamless swapping of art assets later. Near release I will finalize the Creative Guidelines and hire an artist for final release assets, and work to rebuild them into the game. 

I absolutely do not recommend spending thousands on assets early in game development for most people. It's far too likely your vision or practical demands change and you need different assets later on. Get by with the minimum until you are ready for almost ready for an alpha of the full game in my opinion.

comments.author: QuantumWhisker
comments.body:
I built klad ([https://github.com/klad-app/klad](https://github.com/klad-app/klad)) specifically to solve art workflows with AI. I was too frustrated with reroll on gen AI models, and it always looked too much like an ai did it, yknow?

So with klad, it's just a drawing app like any other, except every stroke remains editable like a vector (but is an actual brush stroke!). And it's fully controllable via cli.

This means any agent can draw in it, and you can get it and fix all the details, or add stuff or ask agent to fix a specific thing...

It supports animations and pixelart as well!

I've been using it with great delight for a while now.

comments.author: Exaweft
comments.body:
€2k for ten models is a pretty serious investment, especially when you've still got another ten planned and ongoing updates after that.

I'd be looking at whether you can get more mileage out of the models you've already paid for before committing to another full batch. Shared rigs, interchangeable parts, different outfits or variations might be worth exploring, depending on how different the characters need to be.

I'm all for AI helping with development, but I think the tricky bit with art is getting everything to look like it belongs in the same game. Generating one decent model is one thing. Getting twenty of them to look consistent is another headache entirely. 😂

Are the characters all completely different, or is there enough similarity that you could reuse some of what you've already got?

comments.author: Dasky14
comments.body:
I let Claude use the Blender MCP to make a base model from a reference image without details (like a blank slate with roughly the correct shape), then I add the details manually.  
Also Claude can rig and weight paint models much faster than I can, to pretty much the same quality. So I let it do that too, after which I can animate the model.

I don't use textures in my games because it's mainly low poly art with coloured tris, kinda like oldschool runescape, except a bit higher poly count.

With this I can easily make do with the 20€ monthly sub and nothing else, simply speeding up the tedious parts of development for a very minimal cost.
